strengths: The paper addresses an important auditing problem: determining what aggregate label statistics imply about classifier accuracy and fairness when individual predictions or validation labels are unavailable. Formulating this as optimization over compatible confusion matrices is well motivated.

The baseline-mixture definition gives unfairness an explicit mathematical meaning and supports a useful monotonicity property under merging predicted labels. The binary reduction to finite candidates and one-dimensional searches is a substantive technical idea.

The experiments cover 410 binary classification tasks, multiclass Census and Natality problems, and several applications. The initialization ablations demonstrate improvements from greedy initialization plus local optimization, with matching upper and lower bounds in several cases. Algorithms and a code link aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The mixed accuracy–fairness guarantees have substantive mathematical inconsistencies. Section 7.1 defines its variables as mistake rates but applies τβ(a,b)=βη(a,b)+(1−β)(1−b), thereby penalizing accuracy instead of error. Equation (26) also omits the population weights from its error term. Moreover, Lemma 7.3 bounds the derivative of η while claiming a bound for τβ: a=0.2, b=0.4, c=0.1, d=0.2 gives the stated bound zero, although |ψ′|=0.2(1−β). These issues may be repairable, but the discrepancy calculation and Algorithm 2’s tolerance guarantee require corrected derivations and validation.

Section 7 claims that constrained error minimization is equivalent to selecting an appropriate discrepancy weight β. Weighted scalarization generally recovers only supported Pareto points, and the necessary convexity or other structural justification is absent. Consequently, the interpretation of Figures 7–9 as the complete best-possible tradeoff requires additional proof; connecting finitely sampled minimizers does not establish a certified frontier.

The rare-disease justification for the unfairness measure is overstated. Choosing the identity confusion matrix as the baseline immediately gives unfairness ≤ error. For equally weighted groups with disease prevalence p, zero false positives, and false-negative rates 0.1 and 0.2, the measure is p/18, which vanishes as the disease becomes rare despite the twofold disparity. This does not invalidate the definition, but contradicts the claimed necessarily high unfairness in such cases and weakens its asserted advantage over absolute-difference measures.

The central multiclass experiment with unknown confusion matrices provides insufficient evidence about inference quality. Tables 5–8 report local-search upper bounds on minimum possible unfairness, which cannot establish how much unfairness the aggregates compel. Table 5’s six-label decision tree has an upper bound of 3.20% despite actual unfairness of 0.77%, demonstrating a substantial optimization gap. Corresponding lower bounds, runtime measurements, and initialization/tolerance sensitivity are needed. Trends in Figure 12’s upper bounds alone cannot establish trends in underlying unfairness.

The application conclusions depend on insufficiently examined population and uncertainty assumptions. For example, statewide cancer incidence is combined with Bing-user prediction rates without establishing matching populations or time horizons. Section 4 briefly mentions interval constraints, but the full inference procedures lack uncertainty calibration. The clipping and marginal smoothing in Sections 6.2.2 and 7.2 also alter the inference problem without a bound relating the reported certificates to the original inputs.

Originality relative to the authors’ prior work is difficult to assess. The manuscript explicitly calls itself an extension of Sabato and Yom-Tov (ICML 2020), but does not clearly identify which definitions, binary results, algorithms, and experiments are inherited and which contributions are new. This distinction is especially important when assessing the significance of the multiclass extension.
